szoveg_eredeti:
Nanotechnology and Artificial Intelligence Advance Immunotherapy Against Deadly Brain Cancers

Brain malignancies represent one of the most lethal oncological challenges worldwide, generating substantial global morbidity and mortality despite decades of clinical interventions. According to estimates from the 2020 Global Cancer Observatory, brain and central nervous system cancers caused 321,731 new cases and 248,500 deaths globally within that single year. Epidemiological evaluations spanning the past three decades reveal consistent upward trajectories in incidence and mortality across both sexes and most age groups, with projections estimating an approximate 40 percent rise by 2040. Glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, carries an exceptionally poor prognosis. Standard multimodal therapeutic regimens—combining surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy—routinely yield limited clinical benefits, extending patient survival by only four to six months. Surgical intervention is frequently compromised by the deeply infiltrative nature of glioma cells, while chemotherapeutic agents cause off-target toxicity in healthy tissues without preventing disease recurrence.

The primary impediment to achieving lasting therapeutic efficacy against glioblastoma resides in the anatomical fortifications of the central nervous system, predominantly the blood-brain barrier. Operating within the neurovascular unit, this physiological barrier tightly regulates molecular exchange to preserve neural homeostasis, excluding foreign pathogens while simultaneously preventing most therapeutics from entering neural tissue. Under normal conditions, only select nutrients and small lipid-soluble molecules cross into the brain parenchyma, while baseline immune activity remains restricted to resident microglia. Although tumor proliferation induces localized microvascular disruption termed the blood-brain-tumor barrier, elevated vascular endothelial growth factor expression disrupts tight junctions heterogeneously. Consequently, leaky vascular segments coexist alongside intact, protective vascular zones at invasive tumor margins. Beyond vascular impediments, glioblastoma establishes a cold, immunosuppressive microenvironment characterized by deficient lymphocyte infiltration. Malignant cells actively secrete inhibitory cytokines, including transforming growth factor-beta and interleukin-10, while deploying regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and tumor-associated macrophages to suppress cytotoxic immunity.

To overcome these immune evasion mechanisms, investigators have evaluated multiple immunotherapeutic approaches designed to stimulate anti-tumor defenses, led by immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting regulatory receptor pathways. Tumor cells exploit immunological checkpoints, such as cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 and programmed cell death protein 1, to disable host immune surveillance. Monoclonal antibodies targeting programmed cell death protein 1, including nivolumab and pembrolizumab, and programmed death-ligand 1 inhibitors, such as atezolizumab and durvalumab, have entered advanced evaluations. Landmark trials such as CheckMate-143, CheckMate-498, and CheckMate-548 examined nivolumab in phase III settings, while complementary studies paired pembrolizumab with survivin-targeting peptide vaccines like SurVaxM. In parallel, ipilimumab was evaluated in clinical trials to block cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 and promote co-stimulatory signaling on antigen-presenting cells. Antibodies directed against epidermal growth factor receptor variants, including depatuxizumab and nimotuzumab, have also been investigated. However, while these checkpoint inhibitors established acceptable safety profiles, phase III trials in unselected glioblastoma cohorts failed to demonstrate significant overall survival improvements.

In parallel with checkpoint blockade, oncolytic virotherapy and adoptive cellular therapies have emerged as innovative modalities to induce localized tumor destruction and activate adaptive immunity. Replication-competent oncolytic viruses selectively infect neoplastic cells, inducing direct oncolysis while releasing tumor-derived antigens that prime antigen-presenting cells to trigger systemic immune cascades. Clinical investigations evaluating candidates such as PVSRIPO, a recombinant non-neurovirulent poliovirus-rhinovirus chimera targeting CD155, demonstrated encouraging survival outcomes in phase I trials for recurrent glioblastoma, spurring subsequent combination studies with pembrolizumab. Similarly, the oncolytic adenovirus DNX-2401 demonstrated targeted oncolytic activity and immune activation in phase I trials, advancing into combinatorial testing with temozolomide, interferon-gamma, and pembrolizumab. Concurrently, adoptive cell therapies, particularly chimeric antigen receptor T-cell strategies, genetically modify patient T lymphocytes to recognize tumor-associated antigens independently of major histocompatibility complex presentation. Early clinical trials targeting glioblastoma antigens—including EGFRvIII, B7-H3, IL-13Ralpha2, CD70, and NKG2D—have validated feasibility and safety, showing promising preliminary anti-tumor activity in malignant glioma patients.

Cancer vaccines represent another foundational immunotherapeutic frontier, presenting tumor-specific antigens, tumor-associated antigens, or whole-tumor materials to prime cytotoxic CD8-positive and helper CD4-positive T lymphocytes. Formulations span nucleic acid platforms, synthetic peptide constructs, and autologous cell-based vaccines designed to establish durable immunological memory. Among cell-based approaches, dendritic cell platforms have progressed furthest in clinical translation, highlighted by the phase III trial NCT00045968 evaluating DCVax-L. In this landmark study, combining autologous tumor lysate-pulsed dendritic cells with standard chemoradiation produced statistically significant, clinically meaningful improvements in median overall survival among patients with newly diagnosed and recurrent glioblastoma. Parallel phase II trials using cytomegalovirus-specific dendritic cell vaccines produced long-term survival in nearly one-third of treated glioma cohorts. Peptide-based formulations utilize distinct antigenic targets, ranging from established tumor-associated proteins such as survivin, TRP-2, HER2, and EphA2, to highly specific neoantigens like mutated MMP9 and SLC16A3. Furthermore, mRNA and DNA platforms deliver genetic sequences encoding tumor antigens directly into host cells for in situ expression.

To circumvent these pharmacokinetic and immunological limitations, nanoscale delivery platforms engineered between 1 and 100 nanometers have emerged as transformative tools for brain tumor immunotherapy. Lipid-based nanocarriers, including lipid nanoparticles, synthetic liposomes, and biological exosomes, provide biocompatible architectures capable of encapsulating delicate payloads such as messenger RNA, small interfering RNA, and hydrophilic peptides. Preclinical investigations by Yaghi and colleagues demonstrated that lipid nanoparticles encapsulating microRNA successfully reversed immunosuppression and extended survival in glioma-bearing mice. Similarly, research led by Sayour demonstrated that RNA-loaded DOTAP liposomal nanoparticles measuring 70 to 200 nanometers protected encapsulated transcripts from enzymatic degradation, promoted significant expansion of antigen-specific CD8-positive T cells, upregulated major histocompatibility complex molecules on antigen-presenting cells, and extended median survival in orthotopic models. Grippin and colleagues engineered personalized mRNA-loaded liposomes incorporating DOTAP and cholesterol, demonstrating that cholesterol integration facilitated transport across endothelial boundaries and enhanced myeloid uptake.
